concepts: Normals to a curve and the slope condition
questions.question: The number of points on the curve $y=54x^5-135x^4-70x^3+180x^2+210x$ at which the normal lines are parallel to $x+90y+2=0$ is:
questions.key_idea: A normal parallel to $x+90y+2=0$ means the tangent has slope $90$, so count the real roots of $\frac{dy}{dx}=90$.
solution: The normal is parallel to $x+90y+2=0$, so the slope of the normal is $m_N=-\frac{1}{90}$.
The slope of the normal at $(x_1,y_1)$ is $-\frac{dx}{dy}$, so $-\left(\frac{dx}{dy}\right)=-\frac{1}{90}$, i.e. $\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{(x_1,y_1)}=90$.
Hence $x=1,\ 2,\ -\frac{1}{3},\ -\frac{2}{3}$: four distinct values of $x$, each giving one point of the curve.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count the real roots of the quartic by sign changes (intermediate value theorem) instead of factorising it.
solution: Let $g(x)=9x^4-18x^3-7x^2+12x+4$; we need the number of distinct real roots of $g$ (the tangent slope must be $90$).
$g(-1)=12>0$ and $g\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\frac{15}{16}<0$, so there is a root in $\left(-1,-\frac{1}{2}\right)$.
$g(0)=4>0$, so there is a second root in $\left(-\frac{1}{2},0\right)$.
$g\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)=-\frac{143}{16}<0$, so there is a third root in $\left(0,\frac{3}{2}\right)$.
$g(3)=220>0$, so there is a fourth root in $\left(\frac{3}{2},3\right)$.
These four intervals are disjoint, so $g$ has at least $4$ distinct real roots; a quartic has at most $4$, so exactly $4$.
Hence there are $4$ points on the curve.

useful_results: Normal parallel to $ax+by+c=0$ $\Rightarrow$ tangent perpendicular to it $\Rightarrow$ tangent slope $=\frac{b}{a}$ (here $\frac{90}{1}=90$).
The number of points with a given tangent slope $m$ is the number of distinct real roots of $f'(x)=m$; count them with sign changes instead of factorising.
Vieta check for $9x^4-18x^3-7x^2+12x+4=0$: the sum of the roots is $2=1+2-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{2}{3}$.
A quartic with $4$ sign changes between sample points has exactly $4$ real roots, all simple.

concepts: Distance from a point to a curve (normal through the point)
Parametric form of an ellipse
questions.question: Let $C$ be the largest circle centred at $(2,0)$ and inscribed in the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{36}+\frac{y^2}{16}=1$. If $(1,\alpha)$ lies on $C$, then $10\alpha^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The largest circle about $(2,0)$ has radius equal to the minimum distance from $(2,0)$ to the ellipse, attained where the normal passes through $(2,0)$.
solution: Ellipse $\frac{x^2}{36}+\frac{y^2}{16}=1$; the largest circle centred at $(2,0)$ touches it at a point $P(6\cos\theta,4\sin\theta)$ where the normal passes through $(2,0)$.
The normal also passes through $(2,0)$, so its slope is $\frac{4\sin\theta}{6\cos\theta-2}=\frac{2\sin\theta}{3\cos\theta-1}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Minimise the squared distance directly as a quadratic in $x$ (no normals needed).
solution: For a point $(x,y)$ on the ellipse, $y^2=16\left(1-\frac{x^2}{36}\right)$, with $-6\le x\le 6$.
This quadratic in $x$ has its vertex at $x=\frac{4}{2\cdot 5/9}=\frac{18}{5}\in[-6,6]$.
The largest inscribed circle has $r^2=12.8$, so $1+\alpha^2=12.8$ and $\alpha^2=11.8$.

useful_results: For the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ and a centre $(h,0)$ with $|h|\le\frac{a^2-b^2}{a}$, the largest inscribed circle has $r^2=b^2\left(1-\frac{h^2}{a^2-b^2}\right)$. Here $16\left(1-\frac{4}{20}\right)=12.8$.
Reason: $d^2=\frac{a^2-b^2}{a^2}x^2-2hx+h^2+b^2$ is a quadratic in $x$; its vertex is at $x=\frac{ha^2}{a^2-b^2}$.
If $|h|$ exceeds $\frac{a^2-b^2}{a}$ the vertex leaves $[-a,a]$ and the nearest point is the vertex of the ellipse: $r=a-|h|$.
The nearest point of a curve to an external/internal point $A$ lies on a normal through $A$.

concepts: Equation of the normal and slope of a rational curve
questions.question: If the equation of the normal to the curve $y=\frac{x-a}{(x+b)(x-2)}$ at the point $(1,-3)$ is $x-4y=13$, then the value of $a+b$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The point lies on the curve and the slope of the curve there is $-4$ (the normal has slope $\frac{1}{4}$): two equations in $a,b$.
solution: The normal $x-4y=13$ has slope $\frac{1}{4}$, so the tangent slope at $(1,-3)$ is $\frac{dy}{dx}=-4$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes $-4=\left|\frac{-1-3b}{1+b}\right|$ (an absolute value that is not justified); the sign is fixed, $-4=-\frac{1+3b}{1+b}$, and I added the step $4(1+b)=1+3b$. Result unchanged ($b=-3$, $a=7$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the logarithmic derivative of the product/quotient instead of the quotient rule.
solution: At $(1,-3)$ the tangent slope is $y'=-4$, so $\frac{y'}{y}=\frac{-4}{-3}=\frac{4}{3}$.
At $x=1$ the right side is $\frac{1}{1-a}-\frac{1}{1+b}+1$, so $\frac{1}{1-a}-\frac{1}{1+b}=\frac{1}{3}$.
The point condition gives $1-a=3(1+b)$, so the left side becomes $\frac{1}{3(1+b)}-\frac{1}{1+b}=-\frac{2}{3(1+b)}$.

useful_results: Logarithmic differentiation: for $y=\frac{\prod (x-r_i)}{\prod (x-s_j)}$, $\frac{y'}{y}=\sum\frac{1}{x-r_i}-\sum\frac{1}{x-s_j}$ - far quicker than the quotient rule.
A normal with equation $px+qy=r$ has slope $-\frac{p}{q}$, so the tangent slope is $\frac{q}{p}$ (here $-4$).
Always use both facts: the point lies on the curve (value) and on the normal (slope).
Check of the answer: $y=\frac{x-7}{(x-3)(x-2)}$ gives $y(1)=\frac{-6}{(-2)(-1)}=-3$ and $y'(1)=-4$.

concepts: Monotonicity of a function
One-one functions
questions.question: Let $f:(0,1)\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by $f(x)=\frac{1}{1-e^{-x}}$ and $g(x)=f(-x)-f(x)$. Consider two statements: (I) $g$ is an increasing function in $(0,1)$; (II) $g$ is one-one in $(0,1)$. Then:
questions.key_idea: Show $g'(x)>0$ on $(0,1)$; a strictly increasing function is automatically one-one.
solution: Hence $g$ is strictly increasing, so statement (I) is true.
A strictly increasing function is one-one, so statement (II) is also true.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the symmetry $f(x)+f(-x)=1$, which turns $g$ into $1-2f(x)$.
solution: Hence $g'(x)=-2f'(x)>0$: $g$ is increasing, so (I) is true.
Increasing implies one-one, so (II) is true. Option (A).

useful_results: $f(x)+f(-x)=1$ for $f(x)=\frac{1}{1-e^{-x}}$ (the same holds for $\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$, the logistic function).
$\frac{1+e^x}{1-e^x}=-\coth\frac{x}{2}$ and $\frac{e^x-1}{e^x+1}=\tanh\frac{x}{2}$.
Strictly monotonic $\Rightarrow$ one-one; so 'increasing' (statement I) already forces statement II.
Quotient-rule shortcut: for $\frac{u}{v}$ with $u=1+e^x$, $v=1-e^x$ the numerator $u'v-uv'=2e^x$.

concepts: One-one and many-one functions
Monotonicity from the derivative
questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function such that $f(x)=\frac{x^2+2x+1}{x^2+1}$. Then:
options: $f(x)$ is one-one in $[1,\infty)$ but not in $(-\infty,\infty)$
questions.key_idea: The sign of $f'$ is that of $-(x-1)(x+1)$: monotonic on $(-\infty,-1)$ and $(1,\infty)$, but not on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
solution: So $f$ is strictly monotonic (hence one-one) in $(-\infty,-1)$ and in $(1,\infty)$ (and in $[1,\infty)$), so options (C) and (D) are false.
But $f$ changes direction at $x=\pm1$, so it is not one-one on $(-\infty,\infty)$: option (B) is false.

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve $f(a)=f(b)$ algebraically: equal values occur exactly when $ab=1$.
solution: So for $a\ne b$: $f(a)=f(b)$ if and only if $ab=1$.
On $[1,\infty)$, $ab=1$ with $a,b\ge1$ forces $a=b=1$, so $f$ is one-one on $[1,\infty)$; likewise on $(-\infty,-1]$.
On $\mathbb{R}$: $f(2)=f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$, so $f$ is not one-one. Hence option (A) only.

useful_results: For $f(x)=\frac{x}{x^2+1}$ (or any function of $x+\frac{1}{x}$): $f(x)=f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$, so it is many-one unless the domain avoids reciprocal pairs.

So $\frac{x}{x^2+1}$ is one-one on $[1,\infty)$, on $(0,1]$ and on $[-1,1]$ (a pair with $ab=1$ inside $[-1,1]$ forces $a=b=\pm1$), but not on an interval containing both $t$ and $\frac{1}{t}$ for some $t\neq\pm1$.
$\frac{x^2+2x+1}{x^2+1}=1+\frac{2x}{x^2+1}$ has range $[0,2]$, with maximum $2$ at $x=1$ and minimum $0$ at $x=-1$.
A continuous function is one-one on an interval iff it is strictly monotonic there.

concepts: Integration of a derivative relation
Monotonicity and bounds of a function
questions.question: Let $f$ and $g$ be twice differentiable functions on $\mathbb{R}$ such that $f''(x)=g''(x)+6x$, $f'(1)=4g'(1)-3=9$, $f(2)=3g(2)=12$. Then which of the following is NOT true?
questions.key_idea: Put $h=f-g$: $h''=6x$ with $h'(1)=6$ and $h(2)=8$ gives $h(x)=x^3+3x-6$, increasing, with $h(-1)=-10$.
solution: So $f(x)=g(x)+x^3+3x-6$. Let $h(x)=f(x)-g(x)=x^3+3x-6$; then $h'(x)=3x^2+3>0$, so $h$ is strictly increasing.
Hence the statement that is NOT true is (B).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes $h(x)\in(h(-1),h(2))=(-8,8)$. But $h(-1)=(-1)^3+3(-1)-6=-10$, so the interval is $(-10,8)$. The conclusion (B) is NOT true is unchanged, and now rests on $h(-1)=-10$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Work with $h=f-g$ and definite integrals from the given data points, so no constants of integration are needed.
solution: So $h(-2)=-20$ and (A) is true; $h(1)=-2<0<h\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)=\frac{15}{8}$ gives (C); $|h'|<6\iff x^2<1$ gives (D).
On $(-1,2)$ the range of the increasing $h$ is $(h(-1),h(2))=(-10,8)$, and $10>8$, so $|h|<8$ fails: (B) is NOT true.

useful_results: If $f''-g''$ is a known function $\phi$, then $h=f-g$ is determined by two boundary data: $h(x)=h(a)+h'(a)(x-a)+\int_a^x\!\!\int_a^t\phi$.
For a strictly increasing continuous $h$ on $(p,q)$, the range is exactly $(h(p),h(q))$; it never reaches the end values.
Intermediate value theorem for a root: $h(a)h(b)<0\Rightarrow$ a root in $(a,b)$; with $h'>0$ it is unique.
$h'(x)=3x^2+3\ge3>0$ for all real $x$, so $h(x)=x^3+3x-6$ has exactly one real root ($\approx1.2$).
